newsitem.title: CANADA: Boeing, Airbus battle for Air Canada order.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, Airbus battle for Air Canada order.

text.p: Boeing Co and Airbus Industrie are in a battle for a plane order from Air Canada that could reach US$2 billion, analysts said on Thursday.

Air Canada was expected to announce the plane order early on Friday, shortly after releasing its second-quarter results, which analysts said would likely show a marked improvement from a year earlier.

Jacques Kavafian, analyst at Research Capital Corp, said much of Air Canada's top management was leaning toward awarding the big order to Airbus, of Toulouse, France, but at least one top-level executive favored Seattle-based Boeing.
In the bidding war, two new large capacity jets capable of flying nonstop to Hong Kong from Toronto were being considered -- Boeing's new 777 and Airbus' new version of the A340.
"Everybody in the company was leaning toward the Airbus A340, except for one influential person who was leaning toward the Boeing 777," Kavafian said.
Air Canada was expected to order nine aircraft to replace its aging Boeing 747s, and six more aircraft to provide service on its new trans-Atlantic routes, he said.
At roughly US$130 million for each plane, the order could reach US$1.95 billion.

There has been intense pressure on both aircraft makers to win the bid. Earlier this week, the head of a union representing 1,500 Boeing workers in Canada urged Air Canada to go with Boeing because the company had been a long-time investor in Canada's growing aerospace sector.
Airbus is seen as having an advantage because it sold US$1.8 billion of jets to Air Canada in 1989.

That contract was the subject of a police investigation by Canadian authorities that uncovered no impropriety and which resulted in a libel suit by former Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney against the federal government. Mulroney won the unprecedented suit in an out-of-court settlement.

Airbus is a consortium made up of French state-owned Societe Nationale Industrielle Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Daimler-Benz AG unit Daimler-Benz Aerospace, and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (CASA) of Spain.
Kavafian said one consideration that might sway Air Canada to chose Boeing is whether Airbus can deliver its aircraft fast enough for the airline.
Kavafian said Boeing had been aggressive on pricing the 777 in an effort to halt Airbus' incursion into the Canadian market.

Analyst Ted Larkin at Bunting Warburg said it would make sense for Air Canada to remain with Airbus aircraft to maintain continuity in fleet maintenance and pilot training, but Boeing was known to be competing aggressively for the order.
